# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and a major cause of ischemic stroke, conferring a fourfold to fivefold increased risk of thromboembolism [1]. Oral anticoagulation (OAC), whether with vitamin K antagonists or direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), substantially reduces stroke risk but carries a meaningful bleeding burden and is contraindicated or poorly tolerated in many patients [2,3]. Because the left atrial appendage (LAA) is the source of more than 90% of thrombi in nonvalvular AF, mechanical exclusion of the LAA emerged as an attractive alternative for stroke prevention [4]. Percutaneous LAA closure (LAAC) has evolved over two decades into an established therapeutic option supported by randomized trials, large registries, and guideline recommendations [5].

## Rationale and Anatomy

The LAA is a trabeculated, embryologically distinct remnant of the primitive left atrium with highly variable morphology—commonly classified as "chicken wing," "windsock," "cactus," and "cauliflower" shapes [6]. These anatomical variations influence device selection and procedural success [7]. Stasis within the appendage during AF promotes thrombus formation, providing the pathophysiological basis for closure [4]. Imaging with transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) and increasingly cardiac computed tomography is essential for sizing and excluding pre-existing thrombus [8].

## Devices and Technique

Two broad device categories dominate contemporary practice: endocardial occluders deployed via transseptal access and epicardial ligation systems. The Watchman device (Boston Scientific) is the most extensively studied endocardial occluder, followed by the Amplatzer Amulet (Abbott) [9,10]. The Watchman FLX represents an iterative refinement designed to improve sealing and reduce procedural complications [11]. The LARIAT system achieves epicardial ligation via combined pericardial and transseptal access, offering closure without an implanted endocardial device [12]. Procedures are typically performed under general anesthesia with TEE or, increasingly, intracardiac echocardiography guidance, and require meticulous transseptal puncture technique [13].

## Evidence from Randomized Trials

The pivotal PROTECT AF trial demonstrated that Watchman closure was noninferior to warfarin for the composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death in patients with nonvalvular AF [14]. The subsequent PREVAIL trial addressed early procedural safety concerns and, despite missing one efficacy endpoint, confirmed improved safety with operator experience [15]. Five-year pooled analyses of PROTECT AF and PREVAIL showed comparable stroke prevention with reductions in hemorrhagic stroke and mortality compared with warfarin [16]. The PRAGUE-17 trial extended evidence by comparing LAAC with DOACs in high-risk patients, demonstrating noninferiority for major cardiovascular and bleeding events [17,18]. The Amulet IDE trial established noninferiority of the Amulet to the Watchman for safety and efficacy endpoints [19].

## Registry and Real-World Data

Large registries have corroborated trial findings. The EWOLUTION registry reported high implantation success and low complication rates with the Watchman in a real-world cohort [20]. The US National Cardiovascular Data Registry LAAO Registry, encompassing tens of thousands of procedures, documented procedural success exceeding 98% with declining complication rates as adoption expanded [21]. Comparable European registry data confirmed favorable outcomes with the Amulet device [22].

## Post-Procedural Management and Device-Related Thrombus

Optimal antithrombotic management after implantation remains debated. Regimens range from short-course DOAC or warfarin to dual antiplatelet therapy, with strategies individualized to bleeding risk [23]. Device-related thrombus (DRT) occurs in roughly 3–4% of patients and is associated with increased thromboembolic events, underscoring the importance of follow-up imaging [24,25]. Incomplete closure and peridevice leak are additional concerns whose clinical significance continues to be evaluated [26].

## Guidelines and Patient Selection

Current guidelines assign LAAC a role primarily in patients with nonvalvular AF and elevated stroke risk who have contraindications to long-term anticoagulation [5,27]. Appropriate patient selection through multidisciplinary heart-team evaluation is emphasized [27]. Ongoing trials, including CHAMPION-AF and OPTION, are evaluating LAAC against DOACs in broader populations and in combination with catheter ablation [28].

## Future Directions

Emerging areas include the role of LAAC concomitant with cardiac surgery or ablation, refinements in imaging-guided sizing, and novel device designs aimed at reducing DRT and peridevice leak [29]. As DOACs serve as the comparator in future randomized trials, robust long-term data will define whether LAAC can extend beyond anticoagulation-intolerant populations [30].

## Conclusion

Percutaneous LAAC is a validated stroke-prevention strategy for selected patients with nonvalvular AF, particularly those unable to tolerate long-term anticoagulation. Continued device innovation, refined antithrombotic protocols, and ongoing comparative trials against DOACs will further clarify its evolving role.
